paragraphs: Swamiji told two episodes from Rajput history. The first begins in the ancient city of Kanauj, where a Rajput king had a daughter, Samyukta. She had heard of the courage and glory of Prithvi Rai, king of Ajmer and Delhi, and had fallen in love with him.

Her father planned a Rajasuya sacrifice, a grand ceremony where all the kings of the land had to serve him as their overlord, and he announced that his daughter would choose her husband there. Prithvi Rai, proud and powerful, would not bow to her father, so he refused to attend. In revenge, the king had a golden statue of Prithvi Rai made and placed by the door, as if assigning him the job of a doorkeeper.

Prithvi Rai answered like a true knight. He rode in, swept Samyukta up behind him on his horse, and the two escaped together. Her furious father chased them with his army, and in the battle that followed most of both armies were wiped out. Swamiji said the Rajputs were so weakened that the way opened for Muslim rule in India.

The second episode came as that rule was spreading across northern India. The Queen of Chitore, Rani Padmini, was famous for her beauty. Word reached the sultan, and he demanded she be sent to his harem. A terrible war followed. When the Rajputs could hold out no longer, the men took up their swords and fought to the last, and the women chose to die in the flames.

When the conqueror finally entered the city, he found a great fire burning in the street, with rings of women circling it, the queen at their head. As he approached and asked her not to leap in, she told him this was how a Rajput woman treated him, and threw herself into the fire.

Tradition says 74,500 women died that day to protect their honour. Swamiji added that for this reason people would write '74½' on a sealed letter, meaning that whoever dared open it would bear the sin of all those deaths.
learn: These are hard, tragic chapters of history, and they show how far people once went to protect their dignity in the face of force. The lasting lesson is the courage to refuse what is wrong, and to remember the real cost that pride, rivalry and conquest have carried.
